title: ICE Wants to Use AI to Monitor Detainee Calls and Movements
content:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement is looking for an AI software that can monitor the phone and video calls and movements of immigrants at detention centers.
The system would use transcriptions and voice-recognition technology to monitor who detainees are talking to and the contents of the calls, as well as data from cameras, according to a document the agency posted Friday on a federal government contracting website.
ICE is looking for software that can integrate information it already gathers to generate leads on safety and security concerns and potential criminal activity that an employee would review. The document refers to the software as the “Suite” and it would run 24/7, storing profiles of detainees.
“ICE facilities generate authorized telephone, messaging, tablet, video-visitation, detainee management, movement, incident, and camera data at volumes that cannot be reviewed and correlated manually in a timely manner,” the document states.
Trending
The publishing of the request for information from potential contractors marks a preliminary step in finding a company to provide the service. Watchdog group Project Salt Box first reported on the document.
Immigration policy and data experts raised concerns about how ICE would use the data it could potentially gather to target undocumented families outside of detention. The proposed system is part of an expansion of AI that the Department of Homeland Security is using to track immigrants and citizens during the second Trump administration.
“It’s basically bringing AI into the game of superpowering ICE even more,” said Todd Schulte, president of the immigrants’ rights advocacy group FWD.us.
While ICE already monitors detainees’ telephone and video calls that are not related to legal matters, the software would expand that surveillance through voice recognition. The aim would be to maintain profiles that track whether the person the detainee talks to in any given call is the person the software associates with the number dialed. ICE labeled the person not matching the associated phone number “receiver-side deception.”
Steven Hubbard, a senior data scientist at the American Immigration Council who has been keeping tabs on how the agency is using AI, said such a program could add to mistakes.
“Especially with biometric data, there can be lots of different errors that happen, and then once that is entered into the system, then it becomes sort of a black box where you don’t know how AI is making those determinations or summarizations that can cause problems or create errors,” he said.
Using video camera feeds at the detention centers, the software would need to flag fights, falls, signs of aggression and self-harm, according to the ICE document. During President Donald Trump’s second term, people in ICE detention have committed suicide at an unparalleled rate, according to an Associated Press investigation.
Schulte and David Bier, the Cato Institute’s director of immigration studies, expressed skepticism that ICE would use the software to protect the detainees’ well-being.
“People are committing suicide because they feel hopeless and are cut off from their lives, and feeling like you can’t communicate freely with people on the outside would potentially exacerbate that problem,” Bier said.

report.summary: ICE seeks AI to monitor detainee calls, video, movements, raising civil liberties and accuracy concerns.
report.background: Immigration and Customs Enforcement posted a request for information on a federal contracting website, seeking an AI "Suite" to monitor detainees in immigration detention. The system would integrate authorized telephone, messaging, tablet, video-visitation, detainee-management, movement, incident, and camera data. ICE already monitors non-legal calls, but the new software would add transcription, voice recognition, video analytics, and centralized profiles. The agency says data volumes are too large to review manually. The request is preliminary, part of a broader Department of Homeland Security expansion of AI tracking under the second Trump administration. Watchdog group Project Salt Box first reported the document, and immigration experts warn it could extend surveillance beyond detention facilities to target undocumented families.
key_points: The proposed "Suite" would run 24/7, transcribe phone and video calls, apply voice recognition, and store detainee profiles. It would compare whether the person speaking matches the number dialed, flagging "receiver-side deception." Camera feeds would be analyzed for fights, falls, aggression, and self-harm. This expands existing monitoring of non-legal calls through biometric identification.

ICE says detention facilities generate phone, messaging, tablet, video-visitation, detainee-management, movement, incident, and camera data at volumes too large for manual review. The AI would correlate these streams and generate leads on safety, security, and potential criminal activity for an employee to review. The contracting document is only a preliminary request for information.

Immigration and data experts warn the system could be used to target undocumented families outside detention. Steven Hubbard of the American Immigration Council noted biometric and AI errors can enter a "black box," making determinations hard to explain or challenge. FWD.us president Todd Schulte called it "superpowering ICE even more."

The article notes ICE detention suicides occurred at an unparalleled rate during Trump's second term, per an Associated Press investigation. Critics doubt the software would protect detainee well-being. David Bier of Cato said people feel hopeless and cut off; reducing free communication with outsiders could worsen the problem.

The request is part of a broader Department of Homeland Security push to expand AI tracking of immigrants and citizens. It follows existing ICE monitoring of detainees' non-legal calls, but adds voice recognition, video analytics, and centralized profiles. Watchdog group Project Salt Box first reported the document.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this proposal normalizes biometric and multimodal surveillance in high-stakes immigration enforcement, increasing scrutiny of vendors that supply transcription, speaker recognition, and video anomaly detection. Developers face pressure to address bias, false positives, explainability, and privacy, especially when errors can affect liberty. For regular users and immigrant communities, the chilling effect is immediate: detainees may avoid calls, families may fear contact, and misidentification could lead to wrongful leads, detention, or deportation. The system could also push surveillance beyond detention, turning routine communication and movement data into investigative evidence without clear safeguards or due process.
report.tools: To follow this issue, watch Project Salt Box, FWD.us, the American Immigration Council, and Cato's immigration studies. For technical context on the AI involved, examine OpenAI Whisper for transcription, pyannote.audio for speaker diarization, OpenCV or YOLO for video anomaly detection, and NIST FRVT for face-recognition error rates. These tools illustrate capabilities and risks—not a blueprint for warrantless surveillance.
